gap: No result ChatGPT got states that macOS does not extend displays fed by DisplayPort MST (a single USB-C cable carrying two screens). Those displays mirror. So on a Mac, a dual-screen extender that runs both screens off one cable needs a DisplayLink-type driver, which on macOS needs Screen Recording permission. The driver-free route is one video-capable USB-C cable per screen on a Mac that drives two external displays.
standout_why: I checked the cited Xebec comparison page, the Xebec Dual-Screen 3 help page, the Mobile Pixels Xebec-vs-Trio comparison, Macworld's best-portable-monitors-for-Mac page and itechguides' 15-best list. The Xebec comparison only says the Tri-Screen 3 adapter is 'Required for Tri-Screen 3 use on any MacBook Pro or Air laptop' and never says why. Mobile Pixels' comparison writes 'Mac (Adapter required, sold separately)' and does not mention MST or DisplayLink. Macworld's roundup says plain M1/M2 and Neo Macs are 'limited to connecting just a single monitor' and that the Trio 'Requires software installation', but it never mentions MST or mirroring. itechguides says DisplayLink 'is not equivalent to native DisplayPort Alt Mode' and may need 'screen-recording or accessibility permissions on macOS', but it never connects this to single-cable dual screens or MST. None of these pages explains that a single cable carrying two screens shows a mirrored picture on a Mac. Part of this is on rival pages (adapter needed, software on base chips), so I scored it 2, not 3.
decides: For a day trader on a Mac, this decides whether two separate screens (charts on one, Level 2 and order entry on the other) work at all. ChatGPT's 'premium, compact' Xebec Tri-Screen 3 runs on any MacBook only through Xebec's separately sold adapter, because Xebec says it 'drives two external screens at the same time', which a standard USB-C DisplayPort connection can't do on a Mac. The Trio 3 Pro (ours) runs both screens without software over its two included USB-C cables, one per screen, on an M1/M2/M3 Pro or Max or any M4/M5 MacBook (Macworld, Simon Jary). On plain M1/M2 and MacBook Neo machines it needs Mobile Pixels' free software. That makes the Trio 3 Pro the pick for Mac traders whose Mac drives two displays: they plug in two cables and need no driver. On a Windows laptop with DP Alt Mode, MST and per-port SST both extend. There the pick comes down to screen size and resolution, and the two-cable, driver-free FOPO dual extenders (ours) stay valid. Base M1/M2 Mac owners need a driver-based path whatever they buy. The page should say so plainly rather than call any screen 'compatible with Mac'.

findings.label: MST (one cable, several displays) on macOS
findings.value: Mirrored, not extended: 'MST is not supported on macOS for extended displays'; 'MST-connected displays are mirrored, not extended'. On Windows and ChromeOS with DP 1.2 or higher over USB-C, MST 'Fully support[s] MST for extended desktop configurations'
findings.source_title: Understanding MST: Multi-Display Setups with Windows, macOS, and DisplayPort (Plugable Knowledge Base, updated 2025-03-26)
findings.note: Plugable, a dock maker, in its own words. This is a standards and OS behaviour statement, not tied to one product.

findings.label: Mac video path
findings.value: Not compatible with any Mac without the Tri-Screen 3 Mac Adapter, even on DisplayPort or Thunderbolt 3+ ports, because the Tri-Screen 3 'drives two external screens at the same time'. Windows, Linux or ChromeOS laptops with DisplayPort or Thunderbolt 3+ need no adapter.
findings.source_title: Which USB-C Ports Are Compatible with the Tri-Screen 3 and Dual-Screen 3? (Xebec Help Center)
findings.note: Xebec's help center. The same page says the Dual-Screen 3 (one added screen) needs no adapter on a Mac.

findings.label: Adapter requirement (maker's comparison page)
findings.value: 'Requires the Tri-Screen 3 Adapter (sold separately) for every MacBook Air/Pro' and 'for some Windows, Chromebook, or Linux laptops'; Mac adapter 'Required for Tri-Screen 3 use on any MacBook Pro or Air laptop'; marketed as 'Single Cable Connection'
findings.source_title: Compare Xebec Tri-Screen 3 vs. Xebec Snap vs. Xebec Dual-Screen 3
findings.note: This is a page ChatGPT cited. It states the adapter rule but gives no reason (no mention of MST or DisplayLink).

findings.label: Video path on Mac
findings.value: Two included USB-C cables, one per screen. No software on an M1/M2/M3 Pro or Max or any M4/M5 MacBook (the manual: with 'two DP enabled USB-C ports' driver installation 'is not necessary'). Plain M1/M2 and MacBook Neo are 'limited to connecting just a single monitor' and need Mobile Pixels' free software. Running both screens from a single cable also needs the software.
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Named reviewer quoting the Trio manual. The same review says the screens can't draw enough power from the laptop for maximum brightness; Jary found the capped brightness fine.

findings.label: DisplayLink on macOS: permission needed
findings.value: 'Enable “Screen Recording” to allow the DisplayLink Manager app to capture pixels and send them to your USB peripheral'; 'macOS supports a maximum of 4 virtual displays whatever their technology'
findings.source_title: DisplayLink Manager App for macOS Introduction, Installation & Scope (DisplayLink support)
findings.note: Applies to any driver-based (DisplayLink) route on a Mac, which is how a base M1/M2 MacBook gets a second added screen. DisplayLink also says the screen 'is not actually being recorded'.
